summary: Most visitors do not need a visa for Eswatini — citizens of most SADC and Commonwealth countries, most of the EU and the US enter visa-free for up to 30 days — while the remaining nationalities apply in advance through an Eswatini mission or the government’s eVisa service.

notes: Eswatini is in the Southern African Customs Union with South Africa — goods bought in SACU normally pass freely, but firearms, large cash sums and commercial quantities of goods must be declared.

payments.text: Cards work in Mbabane, Manzini, malls and lodges, and ATMs are easy to find in towns. The lilangeni is pegged 1:1 to the South African rand, and rand notes are accepted everywhere — though rand coins and lilangeni are not usable back in South Africa.

safety.text: Canada advises a high degree of caution because of the risk of civil unrest. Pro-democracy protests have recurred since 2021 and further demonstrations are likely, particularly in Mbabane and Manzini; security forces have used force to disperse crowds, so avoid gatherings. Petty crime, including robbery, is common but lower than elsewhere in southern Africa.

source.name: Government of Canada — Travel advice and advisories: Eswatini

bestTimeToVisit.text: The dry winter from May to September is best for game viewing in Hlane and Mkhaya and for hiking in Malolotja, with mild sunny days; summer brings the Umhlanga Reed Dance (late August/September) and Incwala (December/January) festivals.

tips.text: South African rand is accepted at par everywhere, so there is little need to change money for a short visit, but spend your lilangeni and rand coins before leaving, as they are hard to use or exchange outside the kingdom.

Most land borders with South Africa and Mozambique close in the evening (typically 5–8 pm; Ngwenya/Oshoek and a few others run longer). Check crossing hours before setting out to avoid being locked out overnight.
The standard visa-free stay is 30 days — extensions are granted at the Ministry of Home Affairs immigration office in Mbabane, so apply there before your entry stamp expires if you want more time.
If your dates are flexible, aim for the Umhlanga Reed Dance (late August/early September) or MTN Bushfire festival (May). Book accommodation well ahead, as the kingdom’s lodges fill quickly.
Roads are decent by regional standards, but watch for livestock, pedestrians and unlit vehicles at night, and remember to drive on the left, as in South Africa.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Eswatini?
faq.answer: Most visitors do not — citizens of most SADC countries, most of the Commonwealth, most of the EU, the US and several other states enter visa-free for up to 30 days. Nationalities that do need a visa must obtain it in advance from an Eswatini mission or through the government’s eVisa service; visas are not issued at the border.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Eswatini without a visa?
faq.answer: Normally 30 days, stamped on arrival. You can apply to extend your stay at the Ministry of Home Affairs immigration office in Mbabane before the stamp expires.

faq.question: Can I visit Eswatini as a side trip from South Africa?
faq.answer: Yes. It is a popular loop from Johannesburg or Kruger, crossing at Ngwenya/Oshoek or other posts. You pass full immigration both ways, so make sure your South African visa or waiver allows re-entry, and check border opening hours, as most posts close in the evening.

faq.question: What currency does Eswatini use?
faq.answer: The Swazi lilangeni (plural emalangeni), pegged 1:1 to the South African rand. Rand notes are accepted everywhere at par, so most visitors simply use rand — just avoid ending up with lilangeni or coins you cannot spend after leaving.

faq.question: Is Eswatini the same country as Swaziland?
faq.answer: Yes — the kingdom changed its official name from Swaziland to Eswatini in 2018. Older documents, maps and visa stamps may still say Swaziland; both refer to the same country.

faq.question: Is yellow fever vaccination required for Eswatini?
faq.answer: Only if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Coming from South Africa, Europe or North America, no certificate is needed.
